messages.content: Write the opening pitch section of a README for a new open source charting library. Around 200 words.

# Kestrel

Kestrel draws charts. It won't hold your state, take over your DOM, or hand you a theme system you then have to argue with.

Feed it an array of objects plus two accessor functions and you get SVG back. Every mark — bars, lines, areas, ribbons, anything you write yourself — is a function of scale and data, so a candlestick chart with an annotation layer and a broken axis takes four calls instead of a search through a 400-key config object for the flag that turns it on.

The runtime is 9 kB gzipped and depends on nothing except a d3-scale fork we vendored. Output is a string either way, so charts come out the same on the server as in the browser. Aim one at a Node script and you get an SVG file ready to rasterize. Aim it at React and you get elements.

This exists because we had a dashboard of 60 small multiples, and every mainstream library either wrecked the frame budget or made us write the same 200 lines of margin arithmetic sixty times over.

Want a chart in one line? Use Chart.js. Want to say exactly what the picture should be? Read on.

---

Still to swap before release: the name and the numbers. The 9 kB, the vendored d3-scale fork, and the 60-small-multiples story are stand-ins. Replace them with your real figures rather than cutting them — the concrete detail is what stops this reading like every other library's front page.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

# Kestrel

Kestrel draws charts. It doesn't manage your state, claim your DOM, or ship a theme system you'll spend a week fighting.

Hand it an array of objects and two accessor functions; it hands back SVG. Marks — bars, lines, areas, ribbons, whatever you write yourself — are plain functions of scale and data. A candlestick chart with an annotation layer and a broken axis is four calls, not a hunt through a 400-key config object for the flag that turns it on.

The runtime is 9 kB gzipped, with no dependencies beyond a vendored fork of d3-scale. Output is a string on both sides of the wire, so a chart renders identically in Node and in the browser. Point it at a build script and you get an SVG file ready to rasterize. Point it at React and you get elements.

It exists because we had a dashboard with 60 small multiples, and every established library either blew the frame budget or made us rewrite the same 200 lines of margin arithmetic sixty times.

Need a chart in one line? Chart.js is right there. Need to say exactly what the picture is? Keep reading.

---
